Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage

Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of 
Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchange
Dear Administrator Oz:
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc. (CRCHC) was established on June 14, 2006, 
with a mission “to positively impact the health of our community, one patient at a time.” CRCHC 
operates six active brick-and-mortar sites spanning four counties with both urban and rural 
demographics, two special populations clinics serving migrant and homeless individuals, two 
active mobile buses providing medical and dental services, and a newly established school-based 
care program in Wake County. 
CHCs are the healthcare home for many of America’s medically underserved communities. In 
2025, CRCHC served 19,381 unique patients across 60,779 total patient encounters – with 44% of 
the patient population being uninsured. For these patients, delays associated with prior 
authorization (PA) requirements can interrupt treatment, delay necessary care, and create 
significant barriers to maintaining stable health outcomes. These delays are common under the 
current system. A survey from the American Medical Association (AMA) found that 94 percent 
of physicians reported prior authorization delays patient care, while patient surveys found the 
average wait time for a prior authorization decision was approximately three days, with nearly 
one-third of patients waiting longer than one week for a determination.1 At the same time, PA 
requirements continue to impose substantial administrative burden on CHCs already operating 
under significant workforce and financial constraints. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health 
Centers, Inc therefore supports many of the changes in this proposed rule because of their potential 
to reduce administrative burden and improve timely patient access to medically necessary care and 
prescription drugs. 
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 
2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule. Our comments 
are broken into seven sections:
I.
Interoperability Standards for Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)
1 https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/meet-physicians-newest-allies-prior-authorization-battle 
2
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc appreciates CMS’ continued efforts to 
modernize interoperability infrastructure and improve electronic prior authorization (ePA) 
processes. We strongly support the goal of creating more standardized, interoperable, and real-
time data exchange across payers, providers, and health IT systems to improve patient access to 
timely care. For CHCs, which frequently coordinate across multiple health plan issuers, hospitals, 
specialists, pharmacists, and behavioral health providers, the current PA environment remains 
highly fragmented and administratively burdensome. These proposals to standardize API 
functionality and data exchange requirements could significantly reduce duplicative 
documentation requests, improve visibility into PA requirements, and streamline care coordination 
for medically underserved patients. These reforms are urgently needed, given the scale of PA 
activity nationally. Reports show that Medicare Advantage (MA) Organizations made nearly 53 
million PA determinations in 2024 alone, including more than four million full or partial denials.2 
Similarly, a Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) report that physician practices 
continue to experience substantial staffing and workflow burden associated with manual PA 
processes, contributing to treatment delays and administrative strain across the healthcare system.3
These burdens are particularly significant for CHCs because of the unique patient populations they 
serve and the financial constraints under which they operate. CHCs serve more than 16 million 
Medicaid beneficiaries, over 6 million uninsured individuals, 20.5 million low-income individuals, 
1.1 million agricultural workers, and over 1.5 million homeless individuals.4 Additionally, more 
than 90 percent of CHC’s patients have incomes below 200 percent of the federal poverty level 
(FPL), and many patients experience significant barriers related to transportation, broadband 
access, language services, and specialist availability.5 Delays caused by fragmented PA processes 
can disproportionately affect CHC patients, who cannot afford delays in medication access, 
specialty referrals, diagnostic testing, or behavioral health treatment. For providers operating with 
limited staffing and infrastructure capacity, repeated manual prioritization submissions, varying 
payer requirements, and inconsistent documentation standards divert essential resources away 
from direct patient care and essential services. 
Concurrently, Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc urges CMS to recognize 
that the success of these proposals will depend heavily on vendor readiness, operational 
consistency, and meaningful implementation support for safety-net providers. CHCs often 
lack the financial flexibility or internal IT workforce necessary to rapidly adapt to evolving 
interoperability requirements and frequently rely on a limited number of EHR vendors and/or 
third-party technology partners. CRCHC’s current EHR system does not support the submission 
of prior authorization requests from within the clinical workflow. Providers and clinical staff are 
required to complete PA requests through external platforms including fax, the Availity portal, and 
individual payer portals, depending on the health plan. This fragmented process requires staff to 
manually gather and re-enter clinical information that already exists in the EHR, creating

2024/

duplicative work, increasing the likelihood of errors, and extending the time between prescribing 
and patient access to medication. The absence of integrated ePA functionality is among the most 
significant administrative burdens CRCHC staff face on a daily basis. The proposed rule 
appropriately places obligations for API readiness and interoperability on impacted payers. 
However, absent corresponding readiness requirements for vendors, we are concerned that CHCs 
may face compliance gaps and operational disruption despite acting in good faith. CMS should 
clarify that providers will not be penalized for failures attributable to vendors, 
clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider control. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health 
Centers, Inc further recommends that CMS coordinate implementation timelines closely with the 
Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) certification requirements and establish 
readiness validation or testing before enforcement begins. Inconsistent implementation of APIs 
and varying rollout schedules across payers could undermine the efficiencies CMS seeks to create 
in this proposed rule.6 
CMS should also consider establishing uniform minimum implementation requirements 
across Medicaid Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers, 
including standardized PA data fields, synchronized implementation guide (IG) timelines, and 
clearer operational standards. Without greater alignment across payers, CHCs may face 
fragmented payer-to-payer workflows that increase administrative complexity, create operational 
confusion, and undermine the efficiencies these reforms are intended to accomplish. 
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc is also concerned that the expansion of 
API-based exchange and ePA requirements may significantly increase cybersecurity 
exposure for CHCs, which are operating with a constrained workforce and infrastructure 
resources. The proposed rule contemplates a broad expansion of interoperable exchanges 
involving sensitive patient information, yet many CHCs, particularly those serving rural 
communities, lack dedicated cybersecurity teams or advanced IT infrastructure comparable to 
those of large health systems. While CHCs maintain a dedicated staff, these IT teams are small 
and usually wear multiple hats, meaning CHCs rely on third-party vendors and organizations to 
assist them in maintaining HIPAA compliance and securing their data.7CRCHC operates with a 
lean IT team that manages infrastructure, cybersecurity, and technical support across multiple 
clinical sites. IT staff routinely manage competing priorities and do not have the capacity to absorb 
large-scale interoperability or systems integration projects without external support or additional 
resources. CRCHC does not have a dedicated cybersecurity officer, and like many FQHCs, relies 
on third-party companies and organizational partnerships to help maintain HIPAA compliance and 
protect sensitive patient information. As interoperability requirements expand, CMS must ensure 
that CHCs are not absorbing unfunded costs associated with cybersecurity compliance, vendor 
upgrades, API integration, or ongoing maintenance requirements. To ensure CHCs can safely 
operationalize these changes without compromising patient access or continuity of care, CMS 
should provide technical assistance implementation guidance, cybersecurity and IT workforce 
development support, and dedicated health IT funding opportunities. CMS should also ensure that 
the final implementation framework reflects the operational realities and resource constraints 
under which CHCs deliver care to medically underserved communities.

faq

Ultimately, Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports CMS’ broader 
interoperability goals because standardized, timely, and transparent data exchange can 
improve patient access to care and reduce administrative barriers that interfere with 
essential treatment. However, successful implementation will require CMS to pair these 
requirements with realistic timelines, coordinated national standards, robust vendor accountability, 
and targeted support for safety-net providers. With stronger implementation safeguards and 
implementation support, CMS can ensure these reforms improve care coordination and reduce 
administrative burden while protecting access to care for CHC patients. 
II.
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports CMS’ proposal to establish ePA 
requirements for prescription drugs. We greatly appreciate the agency’s effort to extend 
interoperability reforms to medication access workflows. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health 
Centers, Inc believes these proposals could meaningfully improve timely patient access to essential 
medications while reducing the administrative burden associated with manual PA processes. For 
CHCs, these changes could also improve point-of-prescribing visibility into formulary 
requirements, utilization management criteria, and authorization status, helping providers make 
more informed prescribing decisions during the patient encounter and reducing avoidable 
treatment delays associated with incomplete or inaccurate submissions. 
The proposal to require all impacted payers to support ePA for every drug requiring PA is 
particularly important for CHCs. In community health, medication adherence is vital for managing 
chronic diseases, preventing costly hospitalizations, and improving overall quality of life.8 As 
previously mentioned, CHCs serve 3.5 million patients with diabetes, 6.2 million patients with 
hypertension, 10 million overweight or obese patients, and 3.2 million people with depression and 
other mood disorders.9 CRCHC serves thousands of patients managing chronic conditions 
including diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and behavioral health disorders including serious mental 
illness. In 2025, our patient panel consisted of 2,573 diabetic patients, 4,005 patients with 
hypertension, and 551 patients with heart disease. Furthermore, a substantial number of patients 
require LAI antipsychotic medications such as Aristada, Perseris, Uzedy, and Invega Sustenna, as 
well as patients on HIV medication regimens, and those receiving buprenorphine for opioid use 
disorder – these among many other critical medications. Timely medication access for these 
patients is not discretionary – interruptions in therapy can result in psychiatric decompensation, 
viral rebound, or relapse with serious downstream consequences. This patient population is also 
more likely to experience non-clinical factors of health that can make timely medication access 
critical for avoiding preventable complications and maintaining continuity of care. Cabarrus 
Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc has consistently advocated for improved ePA 
requirements to support operational efficiency and reduce administrative burden when 
implemented consistently and supported by interoperable technology infrastructure.10 Streamlined 
ePA workflows would reduce treatment interruptions, improve medication adherence, and help

PMC9498383.

CHCs coordinate care more effectively for patients managing chronic conditions, behavioral 
health needs, and other ongoing health concerns.
At the same time, Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc urges CMS to address several 
operational concerns with the proposed prescription drug ePA workflows. Cabarrus Rowan 
Community Health Centers, Inc recommends that CMS require payers to expose benefit 
classification information through the Provider Access APIs (via the CRD Coverage 
Information extension) so providers can determine in real time whether a drug falls under 
the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit pathway. We have concerns that CHCs may face a 
significant burden in managing dual workflows across medical and pharmacy benefit pathways. 
Determining whether a medication falls under the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit may not 
always be clear in real time, particularly for drugs that may be clinic administered. Cabarrus 
Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc also requests clarification on how PA 
determinations would apply in situations where a drug is covered under both medical and 
pharmacy benefits. Specifically, CMS should clarify whether a PA approval issued under one 
benefit pathway would also apply to the alternate payment pathway or whether separate 
authorization determinations would be required. For example, extended-release buprenorphine 
may be billed under the pharmacy benefit when dispensed through a pharmacy but under the 
medical benefit when administered in-clinic by a provider.11 Greater transparency in benefit 
classification could improve prescribing efficiency, reduce inappropriate denials, and support 
more accurate claims processing across payer systems. At CRCHC, several medications used in 
regular clinical practice overlap both the medical and pharmacy benefit divide. Buprenorphine 
(Sublocade) may be dispensed through a pharmacy under the pharmacy benefit or administered 
in-clinic and billed under the medical benefit. LAI antipsychotics are administered by clinical staff 
and billed under the medical benefit at the point of care but may also be dispensed through the 
pharmacy benefit depending on payer and care setting. HIV medications including Cabenuva, 
which are administered as long-acting injectables, present the same dual-benefit ambiguity. For 
CRCHC providers managing these complex medication regimens in real time, the inability to 
quickly determine benefit pathway and authorization status introduces meaningful risk of delays, 
denials, and claim errors. 
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc further requests that CMS carefully 
evaluate how these requirements will interact with pharmacy operations, including 340B 
contract pharmacy arrangements utilized by more than 65 percent of CHCs.12 As 340B 
covered entities, CHCs utilize 340B savings to help stretch limited resources to provide affordable 
medications and expanded services for medically underserved patients. Implementation of 
prescription drug ePA requirements will not occur in a single system. It will require coordination 
across entity-owned dispensing operations, contract pharmacies, third-party administrators 
(TPAs), EHR systems, pharmacy management systems (PMS), and payer APIs. That coordination 
can be difficult because PMS and EHR systems may not always be fully interoperable or able to 
exchange complete, structured information in real time. CRCHC operates two in-house contract 
pharmacies: CRCHC Pharmacy and CRCHC Spencer Pharmacy, both of which participate in the 
340B program as contract pharmacy dispensing sites. CRCHC also maintains 750+ contract 
pharmacy arrangements across all eligible sites. CRCHC utilizes Aventi Health as its third-party

administrator (TPA) for 340B claims management, outside of Walgreens and CVS pharmacies 
which are operated by their own TPA systems. CRCHC’s pharmacy management system and EHR 
are not fully integrated, meaning PA determination data, dispensing records, eligibility 
information, and 340B accumulation data do not flow automatically between systems. Staff must 
manually coordinate across platforms, increasing the risk of missed 340B accumulation events, 
ineligible prescription routing, and PA-related dispensing delays. Pharmacy interoperability 
stakeholders have identified persistent barriers, including limited EHR integration, difficulty 
incorporating native FHIR content, terminology, and value-set misalignment, limitations in 
medication data standards, and competing vendor priorities.13 Studies similarly show that 
pharmacy access to EHR data can improve clinical interventions, but implementation remains 
dependent on system access, workflow integration, and reliable data exchange.14 15 
These gaps raise concerns for CHCs because pharmacy operations often depend on accurate 
benefit, eligibility, prescribing, dispensing, claims, and 340B accumulation data moving across 
multiple platforms. For example, CHCs may face operational challenges if PA determinations, 
dispensing data, eligibility information, and clinical documentation are housed across separate 
EHR, pharmacy management, contract pharmacy, and third-party administrator systems that do 
not consistently exchange data in real time.16,17 These disconnects can delay medication access, 
create duplicative work, and increase the risk of errors in already complex 340B workflows. As 
we mentioned previously, CHCs frequently lack the financial flexibility and staff capacity to 
absorb the costs of new workflow redesigns without support. Cabarrus Rowan Community 
Health Centers, Inc urges CMS to coordinate with the Office of Pharmacy Affairs (OPA) to 
provide targeted technical assistance, implementation guidance, and funding support to help 
CHCs operationalize these requirements safely and effectively. With stronger implementation 
alignment and greater transparency regarding benefit pathways, ePA for prescription drugs can 
streamline medication access, reduce administrative burden, and protect continuity of care for 
medically underserved patients.
CMS should also mandate proactive PA expiration notifications to providers via FHIR-
based alerts. Timely notification of upcoming PA expirations could help CHCs avoid 
interruptions in treatment, delays in medication access, and unnecessary administrative burden 
associated with retroactive reauthorization requests. Evidence shows that proactive outreach 
before expiration achieves positive outcomes in 87% of cases compared to only 25% without such 
notification.18  Proactive expiration alerts could improve continuity of care, reduce avoidable 
treatment disruptions, and support more efficient care coordination workflow for CHCs operating 
with limited staff and resources.

At the same time, Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc urges CMS to recognize that 
electronic prior authorization alone may not reduce overall administrative burden without 
concurrent prior authorization reform. Peer-reviewed evidence demonstrates that providers 
using ePA submitted higher prior authorization volumes, spent more total time on prior 
authorization activities, had greater difficulty identifying step therapy requirements, and 
experienced slightly decreased medication filling rates compared to providers not using ePA.19 
This evidence suggests that ePA without concurrent PA reform may merely accelerate an 
inefficient process.20 Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc therefore urges CMS to 
pair ePA technology mandates with meaningful PA reduction requirements, including 
extension of gold-carding to prescription drugs and sunset provisions for PA categories with 
consistently high approval rates.
III.
Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for PA
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc appreciates the agency’s focus on greater 
transparency and timeliness and supports CMS’ proposals to improve communication and 
align decision timelines for PAs. Standardized decision timeframes across payers and clearer 
communication requirements are critically important for the medically underserved patients CHCs 
serve. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc is particularly supportive of CMS’ efforts 
to align PA timelines across all payers impacted by this rule by requiring more consistent response 
timeframes for both standard and expedited requests. Specifically, Cabarrus Rowan Community 
Health Centers, Inc supports the proposed requirements that PA decisions for covered outpatient 
drugs be made no later than 24 hours after receipt of a request, that standard PA requests for items 
and services be addressed within 7 days, and that expedited requests be addressed within 72 hours. 
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc also supports CMS’ proposal requiring QHP 
issuers on the FFEs to provide notice of PA decisions no later than 72 hours for standard requests 
and 24 hours for expedited requests for prescription drugs. These more uniform and expedited 
timelines will help reduce unnecessary delays in medication access and treatment initiation for 
patients with urgent or ongoing healthcare needs.
Delays in PA approvals frequently result in delayed treatment, interrupted medication access, and 
avoidable worsening of health conditions. At CRCHC, providers regularly encounter situations in 
which medically necessary medications are delayed due to PA requirements that must be submitted 
outside the EHR through fax or external payer portals. In one representative case, a patient 
managing HIV with a newer combination regimen faced a week-long authorization delay when 
the PA was submitted by fax and no confirmation of receipt was received; the patient missed their 
scheduled injection appointment as a result. These experiences are not isolated. They reflect the 
systemic gap between CRCHC’s current administrative infrastructure and the real-time 
responsiveness that medically vulnerable patients require. For CHCs serving medically 
underserved populations that already face non-clinical factors of health, these delays can have

serious consequences. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports aligning PA 
timelines across programs to improve efficiency and accountability.
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports CMS’ proposal to require payers 
to provide specific denial reasons for all drug PA denials, regardless of submission method. 
We believe this change will allow CHCs to more efficiently correct incomplete submissions, 
pursue appeals, and resubmit requests without the unnecessary back-and-forth that typically delays 
care. Specifically, requiring payers to explain why a request was denied, identify missing or 
insufficient information, and provide actionable information necessary for resubmission or appeal 
will create a more transparent and navigable process for providers operating under significant 
staffing and operational constraints.
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc also supports CMS’ efforts to improve public 
reporting of PA denials and timeframes. This change is a step towards greater transparency that 
will improve payer accountability and provide policymakers, providers, and patients with better 
visibility. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc strongly encourages CMS to 
publish these required PA metrics in a centralized, standardized, publicly accessible format 
on CMS’ website rather than relying solely on individual plan websites. Centralized CMS 
reporting would improve transparency, support oversight efforts, and enable stakeholders to more 
effectively identify trends in delays, denial rates, and utilization management practices across 
payers. 
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc encourages CMS to expand the proposed 
reporting framework to better capture the real-world operational burden that PA 
requirements place on CHCs and medically underserved patients, beyond the appeal and 
extended review metrics already proposed: For CRCHC, access to granular PA reporting data 
would directly support quality improvement and operational planning. Denial rate breakdowns by 
medication category would allow CRCHC’s pharmacy and clinical teams to identify payer 
patterns, proactively prepare documentation, and target provider education. First-pass approval 
rates would help CRCHC assess where submission gaps exist and whether additional training or 
workflow changes are needed. Reporting on denials overturned due to inadequate denial notices 
would provide evidence to support advocacy for stronger payer accountability. Data completeness 
metrics would help CRCHC and its TPA identify where interoperability gaps are creating 
downstream claims and accumulation errors in the 340B program.
•
Breakdown of denial rates by service type or medication category.
•
First-pass approval rates prior to any resubmission, extensions, or appeal activity.
•
Reporting on denials overturned due to incomplete, inaccurate, or unclear denial notices.
•
Data completeness and quality metrics.
To further strengthen these reforms, CMS should also consider stronger oversight and 
enforcement mechanisms for plans demonstrating persistent delays, inaccurate reporting, or 
patterns of inappropriate denials. Greater accountability, combined with standardized 
communication requirements and timely decision-making expectations, will help ensure that PA 
processes support patient access to medically necessary treatment. Finally, Cabarrus Rowan 
Community Health Centers, Inc urges CMS to establish automatic approval for PA requests 
9
that are not decided within the required timeframes. We believe automatic approval upon 
deadline expiration would be the most effective mechanism to ensure compliance and would thus 
prevent CHCs and patients from bearing the cost of payer delays through interrupted care and 
abandoned treatment.
IV.
Reporting Payer API Endpoints and Associated Information for CMS To Publish
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports CMS’ proposal to require impacted 
payers to report API endpoints and associated information for publication on CMS’ website.  
Having easy access to API endpoints in a centralized location fully operationalizes CMS’ 
interoperability efforts. Currently, a provider must look up each payer’s API endpoints 
individually to use the Prior Authorization API (PA API) to submit a PA request or the Provider 
Access API to request patient data, which can be incredibly burdensome. Having all impacted 
payers’ API endpoints in one place will increase transparency, reduce provider burden, and 
improve the functionality of the reported API endpoints.
CRCHC’s IT department manages infrastructure and support across multiple clinical sites with a 
small team that does not have dedicated capacity for manual API endpoint research or payer-by-
payer portal navigation. When providers or clinical staff need to submit PA requests or access 
patient benefit information through payer systems, they must locate and access each payer’s tools 
individually, often outside the EHR workflow. Centralizing API endpoint information on CMS’s 
website would meaningfully reduce this burden, allowing CRCHC’s pharmacy team to direct their 
limited capacity toward EHR optimization and patient-facing technology improvements rather 
than administrative portal navigation. CHCs often have small IT departments that lack the capacity 
to manually search each payer’s website for API endpoint information. The CHC IT department’s 
limited resources could be better spent on strengthening and developing innovative technology 
solutions that benefit patients, such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and telehealth. App 
developers and EHR vendors also stand to benefit from centralized, easy access to these endpoints, 
improvements that also directly impact patient care, particularly given that EHR disruptions 
currently occur when hard-coded endpoints become outdated. 
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc applauds CMS for the proposed timelines 
requiring payers to report API endpoint information. Existing impacted payers have until 60 
days after the effective date of a final rule, while new impacted payers have until 60 days before 
they begin covering patients under the applicable CMS program. This approach strikes a 
reasonable balance between payer accountability and operational feasibility. We also support the 
proposal requiring impacted payers to update the information within one week of any changes and 
verify that the reported information is updated at least annually. CHC patients strongly benefit 
when the CHC and its vendors have this up-to-date information, as incorrect information can delay 
access to and delivery of care. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc commends 
CMS’ commitment to transparency and encourages the agency to publish API endpoint 
information on its website as machine-readable files. This will help maximize the utility and 
usability of this data. A machine-readable file prevents diverting valuable staff time to the 
interpretation of large amounts of data. As CMS considers the best approach for reporting and 
disseminating this information, we urge the agency to prioritize ease of access for primary care 
10
providers in safety net settings, especially those in rural areas with limited resources, while 
minimizing duplication and unnecessary complexity.
V.
Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, and Payer-to-
Payer APIs; API Usage Metrics
Information about PA for Drugs in the Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports CMS' proposal requiring 
impacted payers to make detailed information about PA requests and decisions for all drugs 
available through the Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs beginning 
October 1, 2027. As discussed, PA for drugs remains a significant barrier to patients receiving 
timely care. Having information on APIs helps identify opportunities to improve them and monitor 
overall usage trends for key features. While we appreciate payers’ independent efforts to improve 
transparency around PA, we applaud CMS for requiring metrics that will hold payers formally 
accountable. We encourage CMS to continue publishing trends in this data and to seek additional 
policy levers to ensure PAs are not inappropriate barriers to care for patients who need it.
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc appreciates the proposed timeframe for 
having PA information available through the APIs no later than one business day after the 
payer receives the request. This change aligns timeframes with the current policy for non-drug 
PAs. We also strongly support the requirement that PA information remain accessible for at least 
one year after the last status update. This is particularly critical for the populations CHCs serve. In 
2024, CHCs provided care to over 1.5 million homeless individuals and more than 1.1 million 
agricultural workers—populations that move frequently and may not return to a CHC for months 
at a time.21 These patients have a limited window of engagement, making it difficult to track 
outstanding PA requests across care episodes. Retaining this information for an extended period 
supports continuity of care and ensures that future providers, accessing patient information through 
the Provider Access API, can quickly understand a patient's PA history and better meet their needs.
New Proposed Reporting Levels and Deadlines for API Usage Metrics
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports the proposal requiring Medicaid 
managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities to report Patient Access API usage 
metrics both by program and by plan. This added granularity will give CMS a clearer picture 
of where access gaps exist and how to target improvement efforts. Medicaid patients represent 
nearly half of CHC patients,22 and nearly 78 percent of all Medicaid patients in the U.S. are in a 
managed care plan.23 26% of the patient population at CRCHC is enrolled in Medicaid services. 
The breakdown of Patient Access API usage metrics by managed care plan would give CRCHC 
greater visibility into which plans are performing well and where access gaps may be concentrated 
among CRCHC’s patient panel. Having disaggregated data helps improve the value of the reported 
data. Additionally, Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports CMS’ proposal to 
align deadlines with reporting periods. Better alignment reduces administrative confusion and 
makes data more meaningful.

Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc also supports expanding the metrics that 
impacted payers must report for the Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and PA APIs. 
Requiring payers to report denial rates, timeframes for extensions, and adjudicated appeals for 
both standard and expedited PAs will meaningfully improve transparency and accountability 
across the system. Beyond the suggested metrics, Cabarrus Rowan Community Health

Although terabytes of health data are transmitted daily, much of it goes unused in practice because 
it is not surfaced directly to users or cannot be incorporated into clinical workflows. Cabarrus 
Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc therefore recommends that CMS track the rate of 
successful API requests, as well as those rejected due to authorization failures or malformed 
queries, and instances where API calls were not received by the requester. Additionally, metrics 
such as structured versus unstructured data in the request response, workflow impact, number of 
calls per query, number of queries per user, and the cost of maintaining each API would help CMS, 
health systems, vendors, and other stakeholders evaluate which APIs deliver meaningful value. 
With this data, CMS would be better positioned to implement targeted policies to address PA 
issues.
Removing Drug Formulary Information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc encourages CMS to reconsider its 
proposal to remove drug formulary information from the Provider Access and Payer-to-
Payer APIs. While CMS suggests that providers already have sufficient access to formulary 
information through payer websites and standard communications, this access is neither reliable 
nor real-time. As Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) increasingly expand the number of drugs 
excluded from formularies, formulary lists can change rapidly, meaning the information available 
on a payer's website may not reflect a patient's current coverage at the point of care. For CHC 
providers, who often serve patients covered by multiple different payers and lack the 
administrative infrastructure to conduct manual lookups across each, this gap is especially 
consequential. A provider who cannot quickly determine whether a drug is covered, or identify a 
covered alternative, may delay prescribing or default to a less optimal option. Retaining formulary 
information in the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs would reduce this lookup burden, 
support better prescribing decisions, and advance the transparency goals CMS has articulated 
throughout this rule. Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc urges CMS to weigh this 
real-world impact on safety-net providers against the administrative burden it cites as justification 
for removal.
Federal Matching Funds
We appreciate the possibility that States operating Medicaid and CHIP programs might be 
able to access federal matching funds to support the new proposals. Cabarrus Rowan 
Community Health Centers, Inc continues to request that CMS ensure safety-net providers are 
prioritized for these funds, if they are available. Safety-net providers, like CHCs, operate on thin 
margins and would greatly benefit from additional funding to help reduce costs such as provider 
training and implementation expenses. Many CHCs are currently under financial strain, with 
nearly half of CHCs operating with fewer than 90 days of cash on hand. The sector's average 
operating margin has turned negative; one in four reporting negative five percent (-5%) operating 
margins. In response to the unique needs of their patients, CHCs invest significant resources into 
training their staff and patients to meet meaningful use and interoperability requirements. CMS 
12
should consider the specific investments CHCs make, including costs, administrative setup, staff, 
training, clinical training, and patient education needs, and ensure appropriate interoperability and 
access.  
VI.
Modifications to HIPAA Standards Related to PA
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc recommends that CMS provide transition 
support to safety-net providers, such as CHCs, during the transition from X12 to FHIR. We 
appreciate and support CMS’ efforts to move away from X12, a legacy system, and towards FHIR 
standards, an important step in enhancing interoperability. However, CHCs and their 
clearinghouses will need to support both standards simultaneously during transition: X12 6020 for 
claims attachments (CMS-0053-F, compliance May 2028) and FHIR/CDex for PA attachments 
(CMS-0062-P, compliance in 2029). This dual-standard burden is real and must be acknowledged. 
As previously mentioned in this letter, CHCs have limited IT staff due to constrained budgets so 
CMS support would help immensely in the transition. Ultimately, Cabarrus Rowan Community 
Health Centers, Inc requests that CMS extend its February 28, 2024, National Standards 
Group enforcement discretion (FHIR PA API as X12 278 substitute) to cover the CMS-0062-
P transition period.24 This would provide relief for HIPAA-covered entities to use a FHIR-based 
PA API in place of the older X12 278 standard without facing HIPAA Administrative 
Simplification enforcement penalties.
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports the use of Clinical Data 
Exchange (CDex) for PA attachments but recommends specific guardrails to reduce 
provider burden and enhance transparency. CDex allows payers to specify exactly what data 
they need and supports multiple formats (C-CDA, PDF, text, FHIR resources). However, CDex 
also creates a mechanism for payers to issue iterative, escalating data requests. Cabarrus Rowan 
Community Health Centers, Inc recommends CMS:
•
Require payers to specify all needed documentation in the initial CDex request (no drip-
feed)
•
Limit solicited-attachment requests from payers to a maximum of two per PA transaction 
before the payer must issue a decision. 
•
Establish maximum response timeframes for payers after receiving CDex attachments.
These actions will set expectations for what the provider needs to share in the initial CDex request 
and limit the burden on CHC providers when providing additional information. This will likely 
lead to more streamlined, expedited ePA decisions, ensuring patient access to crucial health care 
services and prescription drugs.
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports gold-carding for ePA for 
prescription drugs. We appreciate that CMS has already implemented gold-carding for 
DMEPOS, for supplies with a 90% approval threshold with DME Medicare Administrative 
Contractors and within the WISeR model,25 which began in January 2026 in six states. Gold-
carding in ePA will allow certain providers, such as CHCs, who have demonstrated compliance 
with PA requirements to receive exemptions or more streamlined reviews. We recommend CMS 
24 https://www.cms.gov/files/document/discretion-x12-278-enforcement-guidance-letter-remediated-2024-02-28.pdf 
25 https://www.cms.gov/priorities/innovation/innovation-models/wiser 
13
put out guidance formally recommending payers to implement gold card type initiatives and ensure 
that gold carding privileges extend to all items and services for eligible providers, not just specific 
service categories. This will ensure that providers and their patients will experience the full 
benefits of this strategy to decrease unnecessary PAs. 
Gold carding would help reduce the time staff and providers spend on PA. PA is an expensive 
process for health care organizations that, in many cases, significantly restricts patients’ ability to 
access needed care.26 [At CRCHC, the administrative burden of prior authorization falls 
disproportionately on clinical and pharmacy support staff who must navigate multiple external 
platforms to initiate and track PA requests. Because CRCHC’s EHR does not support native PA 
submission, staff must re-enter clinical data that already exists in the chart, extending submission 
timelines and consuming hours of staff capacity each week. CRCHC does not receive 
reimbursement for this administrative work, and the burden is borne entirely by the organization’s 
limited operational budget. For medications requiring frequent reauthorization, such as LAI 
antipsychotics and HIV regimens, the cumulative cost in staff time across a patient panel is 
substantial. It can take weeks to adjudicate the request, resulting in costing hundreds of dollars in 
staff and provider time at a health care organization for a single therapy for a single patient. 
Notably, this effort is not reimbursed and requires valuable staff resources. CHC patients often 
have less comprehensive health insurance plans that require more frequent PA than those of 
higher-income patients. PAs can exacerbate patients’ health care issues and increase the burden of 
PA costs on CHCs, which already provide lower-cost care with fewer resources. Gold-carding 
would decrease these burdens, and Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports 
gold-carding as a strategy to enhance patient access to care.
VII.
Adoption of Health Information Technology Standards and Incorporation by 
Reference
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc supports CMS’ efforts to ensure ONC-
HHS harmonization of health IT standards and specifications but urges the agencies to 
ensure that the HTI-5 final regulations conform to CMS-0062-P regulations. Corresponding 
ONC-HHS standards continue to promote a nationwide health IT infrastructure and federal 
alignment on interoperability and health information exchange standards. However, Cabarrus 
Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc is concerned about how this rule conflicts with proposals 
in the HTI-5 proposed rule. This rule, CMS-0062-P, expands interoperability mandates, 
specifically CRD/DTR/PAS (the HL7 Da Vinci Project Implementation Guides (IGs) that 
automate ePA) v2.2 by October 2027, whereas the HTI-5 proposed rule, published early this year, 
seeks to drastically change the ONC certification program; for instance, it proposed removing 34 
of 60 certification criteria. While HTI-5 retains the ePA criteria finalized in HTI-4 (90 FR 37130, 
Aug 4, 2025), the broader reduction of 34 certification criteria may affect supporting infrastructure 
— such as clinical information reconciliation and security capabilities — that indirectly enables 
ePA workflows. Vendors serving safety-net markets may deprioritize non-required capabilities 
that CHCs depend on for operational readiness.27 
26 https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/practices/costs-prior-authorizations-increase-for-physician-practices-at-alarming-rate 
27 90 FR 37130, Aug 4, 2025
14
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc is also concerned about a temporal gap between 
this proposed rule’s payer compliance deadlines and the availability of certified provider-facing 
technology. CMS-0062-P proposes payer compliance by October 1, 2027, but the EHR 
certification deadlines established under HTI-4 (90 FR 37130) extend to December 2027 and 
January 2028 for the ePA certification criteria at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)-(g)(33). This creates an 
implementation period of up to three months during which payer APIs may be operational but 
CHC EHR systems may not yet have certified modules available to connect to them. During this 
gap, CHCs and other providers cannot be considered non-compliant for failing to use technology 
that 
does 
not 
yet 
exist 
in 
certified 
form.
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc requests CMS and ONC issue joint 
implementation guidance ensuring any final proposals in HTI-5 do not inadvertently 
undercut final regulations within this rule, CMS-0062-P. We recommend that a formal CMS-
ONC harmonization assessment be published before the CMS-0062-P final rule.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments. We are supportive of these provisions that 
will advance ePA, increase timely access to care and essential medication, and promote stronger 
interoperability standard to benefit CHC patients. If you have any questions, please contact Ritchie 
Glaspy, CCO, rglaspy@crchc.org.
Sincerely,
Don Holloman
Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc. (CRCHC); signed by Don Holloman.
- **Stakeholder type:** Healthcare Provider / Community Health Center / Safety-net Provider.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Established June 14, 2006; operates six brick-and-mortar sites across four counties, two special-populations clinics for migrant and homeless individuals, two mobile medical/dental buses, and a school-based care program. In 2025, served 19,381 unique patients across 60,779 encounters, with 44% uninsured.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

CRCHC supports CMS's interoperability and drug ePA proposals because they could reduce administrative burden and improve access for medically underserved patients, but it stresses that implementation must account for safety-net providers' limited IT, cybersecurity, vendor, and financial capacity. It recommends vendor accountability, no provider penalties for vendor failures, payer alignment, cybersecurity and funding support, benefit-pathway transparency, 340B/pharmacy workflow coordination, proactive PA expiration alerts, stronger PA reduction policies including gold-carding, centralized metrics and endpoint reporting, FHIR transition support, CDex guardrails, and CMS-ONC harmonization.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; CMS-0053-F; 45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)-(g)(33); 90 FR 37130 (Aug. 4, 2025); CMS February 28, 2024 National Standards Group enforcement discretion.
- **Standards referenced:** APIs; FHIR; CRD/DTR/PAS HL7 Da Vinci IGs v2.2; Provider Access API; Patient Access API; Payer-to-Payer API; Prior Authorization API; CRD Coverage Information extension; X12 6020 claims attachments; FHIR/CDex PA attachments; X12 278; C-CDA, PDF, text, and FHIR resource attachments; HTI-4 and HTI-5 ONC certification rules.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: API interoperability and safety-net implementation support**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Standardized real-time exchange can reduce duplicative documentation, improve visibility into PA requirements, and streamline care coordination, but CHCs face vendor dependence, limited IT staff, and fragmented workflows.
- **Specific request:** Clarify providers will not be penalized for failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems; coordinate timelines with ONC certification; require readiness validation/testing; create uniform implementation requirements across Medicaid MCOs and QHP issuers.

**Topic 2: Cybersecurity and funding support for CHCs**
- **Provision ID:** PRIVACY-SECURITY / GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Broader API exchange increases cybersecurity exposure for resource-constrained CHCs that lack dedicated cybersecurity officers and rely on third parties.
- **Specific request:** Provide technical assistance, implementation guidance, cybersecurity and IT workforce development support, and dedicated health IT funding opportunities.

**Topic 3: Electronic prior authorization for drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Drug ePA can improve point-of-prescribing visibility and reduce manual PA burden for medications used in diabetes, hypertension, behavioral health, HIV, OUD, and serious mental illness.
- **Specific request:** Finalize ePA for drugs but pair it with implementation support, benefit-pathway transparency, and PA reduction reforms.

**Topic 4: Medical vs pharmacy benefit classification**
- **Provision ID:** MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** Drugs such as Sublocade, long-acting injectable antipsychotics, and Cabenuva may be billed under pharmacy or medical benefits depending on payer and care setting.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to expose benefit classification information through Provider Access APIs using the CRD Coverage Information extension; clarify whether PA approvals under one pathway apply to alternate payment pathways.

**Topic 5: 340B, pharmacy operations, and interoperability**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CHC pharmacy operations depend on EHRs, pharmacy management systems, TPAs, contract pharmacies, and payer APIs that may not exchange real-time structured information, risking missed 340B accumulation and delays.
- **Specific request:** Coordinate with the Office of Pharmacy Affairs to provide technical assistance, implementation guidance, and funding support for CHCs.

**Topic 6: PA expiration alerts and PA reduction reforms**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** ePA alone may accelerate inefficient processes and not reduce total burden; proactive notifications and reduced PA volume would protect continuity.
- **Specific request:** Mandate proactive PA expiration notifications via FHIR-based alerts; extend gold-carding to prescription drugs; create sunset provisions for PA categories with consistently high approval rates.

**Topic 7: Communications, denial reasons, timeframes, and automatic approval**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Denial reasons and aligned timeframes help CHCs correct submissions, appeal, and avoid delays; payer deadline misses should not harm patients.
- **Specific request:** Finalize specific denial reasons regardless of submission method; maintain aligned timeframes; publish PA metrics centrally; expand metrics; create automatic approval when payers miss required timeframes.

**Topic 8: API endpoint reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Centralized endpoint information reduces CHC IT burden and helps avoid outdated hard-coded endpoints.
- **Specific request:** Publish endpoint information on CMS's website as machine-readable files; require updates within one week and annual verification; prioritize ease of access for rural and safety-net primary care providers.

**Topic 9: API usage metrics and PA data through APIs**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; PATIENT-ACCESS; PROVIDER-ACCESS; PAYER-TO-PAYER
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Detailed PA information in APIs supports accountability and continuity for populations that move frequently. Metrics should measure usability and operational value, not just availability.
- **Specific request:** Make PA request/decision information for all drugs available through Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs beginning October 1, 2027; retain information for at least one year; report managed care metrics by program and plan; add API functionality/usability metrics including success rates, authorization failures, malformed queries, unreceived calls, structured/unstructured data, workflow impact, calls per query, queries per user, and API maintenance cost.

**Topic 10: Retain formulary information in APIs**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Oppose / Modify
- **Rationale:** Payer websites and standard communications are not sufficiently reliable or real-time for CHC prescribing across multiple payers.
- **Specific request:** Reconsider removing drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.

**Topic 11: HIPAA standards transition from X12 to FHIR**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CRCHC supports moving from X12 to FHIR but warns CHCs will face dual-standard burdens during transition.
- **Specific request:** Provide transition support; extend CMS's February 28, 2024 enforcement discretion for FHIR PA API as an X12 278 substitute through the CMS-0062-P transition period.

**Topic 12: CDex guardrails and gold-carding**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CDex can support PA attachments but may enable iterative payer data requests. Gold-carding can reduce unreimbursed CHC staff burden.
- **Specific request:** Require all documentation in the initial CDex request, limit solicited-attachment requests to two per PA transaction before decision, set maximum payer response timeframes after attachments, formally recommend gold-card initiatives, and extend privileges to all items and services for eligible providers.

**Topic 13: CMS-ONC harmonization and HTI-5 concerns**
- **Provision ID:** ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CMS-0062-P payer compliance by October 1, 2027 may precede certified provider-facing technology availability under HTI-4, and HTI-5 deregulation could remove supporting capabilities CHCs need.
- **Specific request:** Issue joint CMS-ONC implementation guidance, conduct a formal CMS-ONC harmonization assessment before finalizing CMS-0062-P, and ensure providers are not deemed non-compliant for unavailable certified technology.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S2/S3:** Supports mandatory CRD/DTR/PAS standards but requests synchronized IG timelines, ONC alignment, and readiness validation.
- **S12/S15/S21:** Supports ePA for drugs but asks for benefit classification through APIs, clarification of dual medical/pharmacy benefit approvals, and implementation support.
- **S16/S17:** Supports specific drug PA denial reasons and asks for actionable information identifying missing or insufficient content.
- **S20/S43:** Supports aligned decision timeframes and requests automatic approval when payers fail to meet deadlines.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports centralized API endpoint reporting, one-week updates, annual verification, and machine-readable CMS publication.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Supports granular API usage metrics and recommends additional functionality, usability, and workflow-impact measures.
- **S37:** Identifies implementation challenges for CHCs, EHR vendors, cybersecurity, 340B operations, and payer variation.
- **S44-S55:** Supports FHIR transition from X12 but requests enforcement discretion, transition support, CDex guardrails, and realistic certification/timeline alignment.
- **S60-S65:** Requests CMS-ONC harmonization and assessment of HTI-5 impacts on CMS-0062-P implementation.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to broader PA reform issues including proactive PA expiration alerts, gold-carding, sunset provisions, and step-therapy-related PA burden.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize API and drug ePA proposals with safety-net implementation support.
2. Clarify that providers will not be penalized for vendor, clearinghouse, or EHR failures outside provider control.
3. Coordinate CMS timelines with ONC certification and require readiness validation before enforcement.
4. Establish uniform implementation requirements across Medicaid MCOs and QHP issuers.
5. Provide cybersecurity technical assistance, workforce support, and funding for CHCs.
6. Require benefit classification information through Provider Access APIs using CRD Coverage Information extension.
7. Clarify cross-pathway PA validity where drugs can be covered under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
8. Coordinate with OPA on 340B and pharmacy workflow implementation assistance.
9. Mandate proactive PA expiration notifications via FHIR-based alerts.
10. Pair ePA mandates with PA reduction requirements, including gold-carding for prescription drugs and sunset provisions for high-approval PA categories.
11. Finalize specific denial reason requirements for drug PA denials regardless of submission method.
12. Publish PA metrics centrally in a standardized, publicly accessible CMS format.
13. Add granular metrics including denial rates by medication/service category, first-pass approval rates, denials overturned due to inadequate notices, and data completeness/quality.
14. Establish automatic approval for PA requests not decided within required timeframes.
15. Publish API endpoints as machine-readable files on CMS's website and maintain timely updates.
16. Make drug PA information available through Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs by October 1, 2027 and retain it at least one year.
17. Report Medicaid/CHIP managed care Patient Access API usage by program and plan.
18. Add API functionality/usability metrics and workflow-impact measures.
19. Reconsider removing drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
20. Prioritize safety-net providers for federal matching funds and implementation support.
21. Extend CMS enforcement discretion for FHIR PA API as X12 278 substitute during the CMS-0062-P transition.
22. Adopt CDex guardrails limiting iterative attachment requests.
23. Issue guidance recommending payer gold-card initiatives across all items and services for eligible providers.
24. Issue joint CMS-ONC guidance and publish a harmonization assessment before final rule.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Safety-net readiness, vendor dependency, cybersecurity exposure, fragmented payer requirements, dual medical/pharmacy benefit ambiguity, 340B workflow gaps, ePA without PA reduction, payer delays, poor metric granularity, X12/FHIR transition burden, and CMS-ONC timeline misalignment.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Medication delays, missed HIV injection appointments, psychiatric decompensation, viral rebound, relapse, avoidable worsening conditions, data/security risk, missed 340B accumulation events, duplicative work, claim errors, and unreimbursed staff costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** No native EHR PA submission; reliance on fax, Availity, and payer portals; limited CHC IT staff; lack of cybersecurity officer; non-integrated pharmacy and EHR systems; contract pharmacy/TPA complexity; vendor priorities; certified technology not available by payer deadlines.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** CRCHC served 19,381 patients and 60,779 encounters in 2025; 44% uninsured; 94% of physicians report PA delays care; average PA wait about three days and nearly one-third wait over a week; MA organizations made nearly 53 million PA determinations in 2024 with over four million full/partial denials; CHCs serve more than 16 million Medicaid beneficiaries, over 6 million uninsured people, 20.5 million low-income people, 1.1 million agricultural workers, and over 1.5 million homeless individuals; over 90% of CHC patients have incomes below 200% FPL; CRCHC has 2,573 diabetic patients, 4,005 patients with hypertension, 551 with heart disease; more than 65% of CHCs use 340B contract pharmacy arrangements; CRCHC has 750+ contract pharmacy arrangements; proactive outreach before PA expiration has positive outcomes in 87% of cases vs 25% without notification; 26% of CRCHC patients are Medicaid; nearly half of CHCs have fewer than 90 days cash on hand; one in four CHCs report negative 5% margins.
- **Studies or research referenced:** AMA, KFF, MGMA, HRSA UDS, NACHC, Weitzman Institute, Pharmacy Times, Krauss et al., Murthi et al., Vishwanath et al., Lauffenburger et al., Salzbrenner et al., CMS guidance, WISeR model materials, 90 FR 37130.
- **Examples provided:** HIV patient missing scheduled injection after fax PA delay; Sublocade, LAI antipsychotics, Cabenuva, Aristada, Perseris, Uzedy, Invega Sustenna; 340B TPA/EHR/pharmacy management system disconnects.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** CHCs, safety-net providers, uninsured and Medicaid patients, rural patients, migrant and homeless populations, providers, EHR vendors, clearinghouses, TPAs, pharmacies, PBMs, Medicaid MCOs, QHP issuers, CMS, ONC, OPA.
- **Economic implications:** Significant unfunded IT/cybersecurity/vendor costs; unreimbursed PA staff burden; possible federal matching funds needed; CHC cash-flow strain; risk of claim/340B errors and payer delays shifting costs to CHCs.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible if CMS coordinates with ONC, vendors, and safety-net providers; requires certified modules, FHIR/API readiness, CDex guardrails, endpoint/reporting standardization, and cybersecurity support.
- **Patient care impact:** Strongly positive if implemented with support; risk of treatment interruptions and access barriers if implementation is fragmented or underfunded.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with substantial implementation conditions
- **Tone:** Detailed, evidence-based, safety-net focused, constructive
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc therefore supports many of the changes in this proposed rule because of their potential to reduce administrative burden and improve timely patient access." - Context: Overall position.
2. "CMS should clarify that providers will not be penalized for failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider control." - Context: Vendor readiness recommendation.
3. "Electronic prior authorization alone may not reduce overall administrative burden without concurrent prior authorization reform." - Context: Concern about ePA accelerating inefficient processes.
4. "Cabarrus Rowan Community Health Centers, Inc urges CMS to establish automatic approval for PA requests that are not decided within the required timeframes." - Context: Enforcement/timeframe recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Raises CMS/ONC timing gaps and asks for readiness validation before enforcement.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Emphasizes CHC budget constraints, implementation costs, unreimbursed staff burden, and funding needs.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Extensive discussion of fax, payer portals, duplicate data entry, and manual PA work.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Flags increased cybersecurity exposure and limited CHC cybersecurity staffing.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Focuses on Medicaid, uninsured, homeless, migrant, low-income, rural, and medically underserved populations.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Addresses EHR readiness, vendor capacity, APIs, CDex, FHIR, and implementation validation.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Discusses CRD/DTR/PAS v2.2, HTI-4/HTI-5, certification timing, and CMS-ONC harmonization.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central purpose is timely medication and care access.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for CMS, ONC, OPA, vendors, payers, CHCs, pharmacies, and TPAs to coordinate.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Requests benefit classification and cross-pathway PA clarification.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports denial reasons, public metrics, endpoint reporting, and formulary information in APIs.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not primarily about small payers, but emphasizes small/safety-net provider capacity constraints.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Details current EHR, pharmacy, 340B, fax, portal, and payer workflows.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Significant focus on EHR vendors, clearinghouses, TPAs, PBMs, and certified technology readiness.
